chapter_title: Mycobacterium marinum Infection: Fish Tank Granuloma

section_summaries.epidemiology: Mycobacterium marinum is an environmental mycobacterium ubiquitous in fresh, brackish, and sea waters. The disease is uncommon and usually presents as sporadic individual cases, although outbreaks involving dozens of individuals have been reported. It can be acquired in fresh or sea water, most commonly when handling fresh water in aquaria or when harvesting. Infection represents an occupational risk for biologists, veterinary doctors, and fishermen.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Inoculation of M. marinum occurs through skin abrasion or injury while handling infected fish or water. Skin lesions appear 2 to 8 weeks after inoculation, spreading proximally on the affected limb, often developing sporotrichoid nodules. Spontaneous resolution and relapse are not uncommon. Glycin-rich proteins contribute to bacterial virulence. Histologic examination may reveal chronic, non-specific inflammation or a mixed inflammatory picture with granuloma formation, and in advanced cases, well-formed epithelioid tuberculoid granulomas, with intra-cellular acid-fast bacilli sometimes observed.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Clinical signs manifest 2 to 8 weeks after exposure, typically starting as a single erythematous papule or small nodule with a smooth or warty surface at the inoculation site, commonly on a finger. Dissemination along the lymphatic track can lead to sporotrichoid nodules on fingers, hands, and upper limbs. Lesions are usually asymptomatic but can become tender and pyogenic if suprainfection occurs. Immunocompromised individuals may experience extensive skin involvement, frank dissemination, septic arthritis, nose and facial mutilation, and nodular vasculitis.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds, considering appropriate exposures, typical clinical manifestations, duration, histology, and microbiology. The history of exposure, typical skin lesions, and granulomatous inflammation on histology are gold standards. Isolation or identification of M. marinum in the laboratory confirms the etiologic diagnosis, though it can be difficult. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays are also available. Differential diagnoses include sporotrichosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, sarcoidosis, and cutaneous tuberculosis.
section_summaries.treatment: Therapy usually involves combinations of clarithromycin and ethambutol or rifampin, administered for 1 to 2 months after resolution, with treatment courses typically lasting 3 to 4 months. Relapse is not uncommon. M. marinum is a multi-drug-resistant organism. Simple localized disease may be treated with single agents like clarithromycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or doxycycline, though most experts prefer two agents. Cure is achieved in approximately 85% of cases with combination therapies including rifampin, ethambutol, tetracyclines, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, amikacin, or imipenem.
